newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Rival Cambodian rebels clash, Pol Pot still at large.
newsitem.headline: Rival Cambodian rebels clash, Pol Pot still at large.

text.p: Former comrades of Khmer Rouge strongman Pol Pot clashed with a band of fighters protecting the ageing communist in remote northern jungle on Friday but failed in their bid to capture him, a government army general said.

First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said earlier on Friday that a final assault on Pol Pot and a handful of his loyalists was imminent, and the prince said he was hopeful Pol Pot would be caught alive and brought to justice.
"Pol Pot has not been captured yet and he has not surrendered yet," Major General Tom Sombol, a top military adviser to the prince, told Reuters.
"There have been some small clashes between Khmer Rouge defectors and Pol Pot's supporters because the defectors are trying to capture him," he said.

Ranariddh told reporters earlier that the 69-year-old Pol Pot was holed up with his last 15 supporters in a stronghold ringed by land mines after a breakaway group of his fighters rejected his offer of surrender.

"They finally know where he is and will make a final assault today in the hope we will be able to capture Pol Pot alive," Ranariddh said. "Pol Pot offered to surrender but the forces around him don't want him to surrender."
But Ranariddh's co-premier and political rival, Hun Sen, dismissed the report that Pol Pot might be captured alive as a political ploy.
"This is a political game," Hun Sen told reporters. He said all top Khmer Rouge leaders should be arrested and imprisoned.
The two premiers, who share power in a rocky coalition formed after U.N.-sponsored polls in 1993, were headed for a showdown over policy toward the rebels, political analysts said.

Ranariddh's royalist party wants to strike a deal with more moderate elements in the crumbling guerrilla force, a move that Hun Sen sees as a threat to his strength in the run-up to polls next year, political analysts said.

But the analysts said that before Ranariddh can shake hands across the bargaining table with less-despised members of the Khmer Rouge, he must be able to assure the Cambodian people -- and the world -- that Pol Pot is finished.
Hun Sen has branded all contact with the Khmer Rouge illegal and told Ranariddh earlier this week to choose between working with him in their coalition or joining the rebels.

"We have some intelligence sources which indicate that this is all play," said a source in Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party when asked of Ranariddh's report of the imminent capture of Pol Pot. "So far we think it's not true".

Ranariddh said Pol Pot would not be allowed to surrender and should be brought before an international tribunal to answer for the death of more than one million Cambodians during his 1975-79 "killing fields" rule.

"There is a great difference between surrender and capture," Ranariddh said, when asked why the Khmer Rouge turncoats would not accept Pol Pot's surrender. "Surrender means we have to give Pol Pot safe conduct. We have to capture him alive."

Ranariddh said Pol Pot's former comrades were proceeding cautiously as they closed in on him because his mountainous jungle position was protected by landmines and because they feared Pol Pot might take his own life.
Pol Pot fled north from Anlong Veng earlier this month after executing his defence chief Son Sen and 11 of his family members, the prince said.
